Doctor: Good to see you again. I have you down as a 58-year-old male, about three weeks out from the hospital stay for the bone infection in your left foot. How are you feeling?
Patient: Better, I think. The foot is less sore. I'm still getting the IV antibiotic through the line in my arm.
Doctor: Right, the PICC line. Remind me what you're getting and how often.
Patient: Cefazolin, two grams, three times a day. The home nurse showed me how to hook it up.
Doctor: Good. Any fevers or chills?
Patient: No fevers, no chills.
Doctor: Any redness, swelling, or pain around the PICC site?
Patient: No, the arm looks fine.
Doctor: How about the foot wound? Any pus or bad smell?
Patient: A little clear drainage on the dressing in the morning, but no pus and no smell.
Doctor: Any diarrhea, rash, or nausea from the antibiotic?
Patient: No diarrhea, no rash. A little nausea sometimes, mostly in the evening.
Doctor: Okay. Let's go through your other medicines. Last time you were taking insulin glargine at night. What dose?
Patient: Thirty units. Actually, no, sorry, twenty units. The thirty was what I took before the hospital stay. They lowered it to twenty when I was in there.
Doctor: Good, so twenty units at night is correct. And your sugars at home?
Patient: Mornings are 150 to 180 or so. Sometimes 200 after dinner.
Doctor: That's higher than I'd like with a bone infection. And metformin?
Patient: Metformin 1000 milligrams twice a day, same as before.
Doctor: Still taking lisinopril 10 milligrams and the baby aspirin, 81 milligrams?
Patient: Yes, both every morning. I stopped the oxycodone, I haven't needed it for a week. And I quit the ibuprofen like you told me when I left the hospital.
Doctor: Now, any over-the-counter supplements or herbal products? I know you were taking a few.
Patient: Yes. I take turmeric capsules, 500 milligrams twice a day, for my joint aches. Fish oil, one capsule daily. And a zinc and vitamin C supplement that a friend recommended.
Doctor: Okay, I'll come back to that. Your labs from this morning: the white count is 7.2, creatinine is 1.3, up from 1.1 last week, and your liver enzymes are a little high, AST 58 and ALT 71. Your ESR has come down from 62 to 38, and the CRP from 4.1 to 1.8.
Patient: So the infection is getting better?
Doctor: The inflammation markers say yes. Let me look at you. Your blood pressure is 136 over 82, pulse 78, temperature 98.4. The PICC site is clean and dry, with no redness and no swelling. The wound on the bottom of your left foot has pink granulation tissue, about two centimeters, a little clear drainage, no pus, and no redness spreading beyond the edge. It is not tender when I press over the bone.
Doctor: To summarize, you have osteomyelitis of the left second metatarsal from MSSA, which showed on the MRI and the bone biopsy in the hospital, and it is improving on IV cefazolin. Your diabetes is not at goal, and you have mild liver enzyme elevation that I suspect is from the turmeric. Here is the plan. Continue cefazolin 2 grams IV every 8 hours through the PICC to finish six weeks total, so about three more weeks. Stop the turmeric today, and stop the zinc and vitamin C supplement too. The fish oil can continue. We will increase insulin glargine from 20 to 24 units at night, and keep metformin at 1000 mg twice a day. No more oxycodone or ibuprofen. We will check a CBC, ESR, CRP, and liver tests every week, and repeat the liver tests in one week to make sure they come down. Please see podiatry in two weeks and wear the offloading shoe, and come back to see me in two weeks. Call us for fever, spreading redness, or any problem with the PICC line.
Patient: Okay. I'll throw the turmeric out tonight.

The patient is a 34-year-old male seen in orthopedic clinic for follow-up of a right rotator cuff tear. He works as a warehouse loader and first noticed right shoulder pain about eight weeks ago after lifting a heavy pallet overhead. He describes a deep ache in the lateral shoulder that wakes him at night when he rolls onto the right side, along with weakness when reaching overhead. He denies numbness, tingling, neck pain, or shoulder instability. He has not had fever or any prior shoulder surgery.

Since his last visit he has attended only one of four scheduled physical therapy sessions. He depends on the bus, the trip takes about ninety minutes each way, and he has lost work shifts to attend visits. We discussed that transportation is the main barrier to his follow-up and rehabilitation.

Medical history is notable for hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril 10 mg daily. For the shoulder pain he has been taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily, which he received from urgent care.

On examination today his blood pressure is 148/92, heart rate 76, and he is afebrile. There is mild supraspinatus atrophy on the right. Passive range of motion is full, but active elevation is limited to about 120 degrees by pain, with a painful arc between 90 and 120 degrees. Hawkins and empty can tests are positive, and supraspinatus strength is 4/5. The Spurling test is negative, and sensation and distal pulses are intact.

An MRI of the right shoulder obtained last month shows a partial-thickness articular-sided supraspinatus tear involving roughly 40 percent of the tendon thickness, mild infraspinatus tendinosis, no retraction, and no labral tear. Radiographs today show a type II acromion with no fracture or arthritis.

Impression is a right rotator cuff tear, partial thickness, with ongoing pain and weakness, and elevated blood pressure that is likely aggravated by naproxen in the setting of hypertension. After verbal consent, a subacromial corticosteroid injection with triamcinolone 40 mg and lidocaine 1 percent was performed today and he tolerated it well. I am stopping naproxen and starting acetaminophen 1,000 mg every 8 hours as needed. He will continue lisinopril 10 mg daily and have his blood pressure rechecked by his primary care clinic within two weeks. He was given a home exercise program with a resistance band, and we will arrange telehealth physical therapy visits so that he does not need to travel. Social work will help him apply for the non-emergency medical transportation benefit through his insurance. A video check-in will occur in two weeks and an in-person visit in six weeks, scheduled on a day when he already has transportation. If he is not improving by three months we will discuss surgical repair. He should call sooner for worsening weakness or numbness.

The impression was a right rotator cuff tear plus hypertension aggravated by naproxen. A subacromial triamcinolone and lidocaine injection was given, naproxen was stopped, acetaminophen was started, and telehealth physical therapy and a transportation benefit were arranged because bus travel limits his follow-up.

The patient is a 17-year-old male seen in dermatology clinic with his mother for follow-up of moderate plaque psoriasis, now four months into treatment with adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every other week. He reports that the plaques on his elbows, knees, and lower back are much thinner and less red than before he started the biologic. He still has scaly patches along the scalp margin and a few thick plaques on both shins that cause itching, particularly at night. His mother helps with the injections and he has not missed a dose. He has also been using clobetasol 0.05% ointment twice daily on the shin plaques for the past three weeks without a break. He has mild acne on the face and upper back and uses benzoyl peroxide 5% wash daily, which he feels is stable.

He denies joint pain, morning stiffness, fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and low mood. There have been no recent infections and no travel.

Vital signs today are blood pressure 112/68 and heart rate 68, weight 72 kg. On examination the elbow and knee plaques are thin and minimally erythematous, there are scaly erythematous patches at the scalp margin, and three thick well-demarcated plaques remain on the shins. Body surface area involved is about 4 percent and the PASI is 4.2, down from 13.5 at baseline. There is no nail pitting, no dactylitis, and no joint swelling. Scattered comedones and a few inflammatory papules are present on the forehead and upper back. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold test done two weeks ago was negative, and ALT was 22 with a normal CBC.

Impression is moderate plaque psoriasis with a good but incomplete response to adalimumab, with persistent scalp psoriasis and shin plaques, along with stable mild acne. He has been on clobetasol continuously for longer than the recommended two weeks, so I am reducing clobetasol 0.05% ointment from twice daily to weekends only and starting calcipotriene 0.005% cream twice daily on weekdays for the shin and elbow plaques. He will continue adalimumab 40 mg every other week and benzoyl peroxide 5% wash daily. We reviewed that he should avoid live vaccines, receive the inactivated influenza vaccine, and use gentle emollients and sun protection. Repeat TB screening will be done yearly. He will return in three months, sooner for joint pain, signs of infection, or worsening skin disease.

The patient is a 75-year-old female seen in the geriatrics clinic for follow-up of mild cognitive impairment, accompanied by her daughter, who provides collateral history. Over the past year the patient has noticed that she misplaces her glasses and keys, repeats questions, and has trouble recalling the names of acquaintances. Her daughter confirms that these changes have been gradual and have not clearly worsened in the last six months. The patient still manages her own pillbox, pays her bills on time, and drives locally in the daytime.

She denies getting lost in familiar places, hallucinations, falls, urinary incontinence, and low mood. Her daughter has not noticed any personality change. She sleeps poorly and has been taking over-the-counter diphenhydramine 25 mg nightly for several years.

Past medical history includes hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily, and hyperlipidemia, treated with atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. She has no known drug allergies.

On examination blood pressure is 138/76 and heart rate 70, and weight is stable. She is pleasant and cooperative with fluent speech. Her MoCA score today is 23/30, with lost points mainly for delayed recall (2 of 5 words) and one point for attention. Cranial nerves are intact, strength and tone are normal, and gait is steady with a timed up and go of 10 seconds. An MRI of the brain done last month showed mild generalized atrophy and a few scattered white matter hyperintensities, with no infarct, mass, or hydrocephalus. TSH was 2.1 and vitamin B12 level was 290 pg/mL, which is low-normal.

Impression is stable mild cognitive impairment, amnestic type, with likely contributions from long-term anticholinergic medication use and borderline vitamin B12. Hypertension is controlled and insomnia is present. I advised stopping diphenhydramine because of its anticholinergic effects, and we reviewed sleep hygiene as an alternative. I am starting cyanocobalamin 1,000 mcg daily. She will continue amlodipine 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. I am referring her for formal neuropsychological testing and encouraged regular walking and social activity. We discussed driving safety, and she will limit driving to familiar daytime routes. Her daughter will help review advance directives. A repeat MoCA will be done in six months, sooner if memory or function declines.

MoCA was 23/30, brain MRI showed mild atrophy with scattered white matter hyperintensities, and vitamin B12 was low-normal at 290 pg/mL. The impression was stable mild cognitive impairment with likely contributions from nightly diphenhydramine and borderline vitamin B12. Diphenhydramine was stopped, cyanocobalamin was started, and neuropsychological testing, driving counseling and a repeat MoCA in six months were arranged.

Hospital day 3 for this 72-year-old female with long-standing type 1 diabetes managed with an insulin pump, who was admitted after an episode of severe hypoglycemia at work. She works part-time as a hospital unit clerk on a rotating schedule of three night shifts and two day shifts per week with changing start times. Her coworker found her sweating and confused during a night shift, and EMS recorded a fingerstick glucose of 38 mg/dL. She received IV dextrose with prompt recovery and was admitted for evaluation and pump adjustment.

Overnight there was no further severe hypoglycemia. Her continuous glucose monitor showed a low of 68 mg/dL at about three in the morning, which she treated with 15 grams of juice, and the low alert sounded as programmed. She denies chest pain, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and alcohol use, and she reports no pump alarms or site problems.

She has had type 1 diabetes for over 40 years, with hypoglycemia unawareness, diabetic retinopathy, diabetic neuropathy, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, hypothyroidism, and hyperlipidemia. Home medications are insulin aspart by pump, metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. Her outside records listed the overnight basal rate as 0.9 units per hour, but the pump download shows it was 1.1 units per hour; the correct overnight basal rate is 1.1 units per hour, not 0.9. The download also shows an insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio of 1 to 8. On the day of the event she worked a day shift, slept only two hours, started a night shift, and took a meal bolus that she then did not finish while the overnight basal continued at full rate.

Vital signs today are temperature 98.2 F, heart rate 68, blood pressure 126/72, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She is alert and oriented with no focal deficits. The abdominal pump site is clean without erythema. Monofilament sensation is reduced in both feet. Laboratory data show A1c 6.4%, creatinine 1.2 with eGFR 47, potassium 4.4, sodium 139, TSH 2.8, and AM cortisol 15 mcg/dL. C-peptide is undetectable, consistent with her diagnosis. Continuous glucose monitor data over the past two weeks show time in range 61 percent, time below 70 mg/dL 14 percent, and time below 54 mg/dL 5 percent, with most lows between midnight and 5 in the morning on night-shift days.

Assessment is type 1 diabetes with frequent, severe hypoglycemia and hypoglycemia unawareness. Contributing factors are overly tight control for her age and comorbidities, a single pump profile that does not match her irregular work schedule, and metoprolol, which can mask the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia.

For management, I am reducing the overnight basal rate from 1.1 to 0.8 units per hour and changing the insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio from 1 to 8 to 1 to 10. We will build two pump profiles, one for day-shift days and one for night-shift days, that she can switch herself, with a higher glucose target on night shifts. The monitor low alert threshold will be raised to 80 mg/dL with the predictive low alert on and automatic suspend before low enabled. The new A1c goal is below 7.5 percent. I am discontinuing metoprolol tartrate and starting amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure. She will receive glucagon nasal 3 mg as needed for severe hypoglycemia, and her family and a coworker will be taught how to use it. Lisinopril 10 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly continue unchanged. The diabetes educator and dietitian will see her today for shift-work meal planning and hypoglycemia unawareness training, and she was advised not to drive if her glucose is below 90. Social work will help with a letter requesting a more regular schedule from her employer. She will follow up with endocrinology in one week, with a BMP recheck, and with ophthalmology as scheduled. Discharge is anticipated tomorrow if there are no further lows.

The overnight basal rate was reduced to 0.8 units per hour, separate day and night shift profiles were built, metoprolol was stopped, and amlodipine and glucagon were started.

Reason for visit: follow-up of persistent asthma that has been poorly controlled.

History: The patient is a 44-year-old male with persistent asthma and allergic rhinitis. Over the past six weeks his control has worsened, with nighttime cough and wheeze about three nights a week, chest tightness, and shortness of breath when climbing one flight of stairs. He uses albuterol about five times a week, and his Asthma Control Test score is 14, down from 19 at his last visit. Triggers include dust exposure during a home renovation, a friend's cat, and a recent cold that has now resolved. He denies fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, and leg swelling, and he has had no emergency department visits or hospitalizations.

Medications: fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 mcg one inhalation twice daily, montelukast 10 mg nightly, albuterol 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed, and cetirizine 10 mg daily. On camera he demonstrated his inhaler technique: he does not use a spacer and does not fully exhale before the dose.

Home measurements: peak flow 380 L/min (personal best 520 L/min), home pulse oximeter 96% on room air, pulse 78.

Video exam: He speaks in full sentences without audible wheeze during the visit, with no accessory muscle use and no cyanosis. No oral thrush visible.

Impression: Persistent asthma, poorly controlled, with allergic rhinitis and a resolving viral upper respiratory infection as a recent trigger.

Management: Step up inhaled therapy by increasing fluticasone-salmeterol from 250/50 mcg to 500/50 mcg, one inhalation twice daily, with mouth rinsing after each use. Start prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days. Continue montelukast 10 mg nightly and cetirizine 10 mg daily. Use albuterol 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed with a spacer; correct inhaler technique was reviewed on camera. Spirometry in clinic in 4 weeks. Reduce trigger exposure with a dust mask during the renovation and avoiding the cat. The written action plan was reviewed. Follow-up video visit in 4 weeks. He should go to the emergency department if peak flow falls below 250 L/min, if he needs albuterol more often than every 4 hours, or if he has trouble speaking.
